'''Leo Moser''' (11 April 1921 – 9 February 1970) was an [[Austria]]n-[[Canadians|Canadian]] mathematician, best known for his [[Moser polygon notation|polygon notation]].

A native of [[Vienna]], Leo Moser immigrated with his parents to [[Canada]] at the age of three. He received his [[Bachelor of Science]] degree from the [[University of Manitoba]] in 1943, and a [[Master of Science]] from the [[University of Toronto]] in 1945. After two years of teaching he went to the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill|University of North Carolina]] to complete a [[PhD]], supervised by [[Alfred Brauer]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=13219}}</ref> There, in 1950, he began suffering recurrent [[heart disease|heart problems]].  He took a position at Texas Technical College for one year, and joined the faculty of the [[University of Alberta]] in 1951, where he remained until his death at the age of 48.

In 1966, Moser posed the question "What is the region of smallest area which will accommodate every planar arc of length one?"<ref>W. Moser, G. Bloind, V. Klee, C. Rousseau, J. Goodman, B. Monson, J. Wetzel, L. M. Kelly7, G. Purdy, and J Wilker, Fifth edition, ''Problems in Discrete Geometry'', McGill University, Montreal, 1980</ref>  Rephrased to consider the planar arc a "worm", this became known as [[Moser's worm problem]]<ref name="Brass Moser Pach 2010 p. ">{{cite book | last=Brass | first=Peter | last2=Moser | first2=William O. J. | last3=Pach | first3=János | title=Research Problems in Discrete Geometry | publisher=Springer | date=2010-10-29 | isbn=978-1-4419-2016-4 | page=458}}</ref> and as of 2026 remains an [[List of unsolved problems in mathematics|open problem]].
